\chapter{Ojala --- a Prayer That Outlived Its Religion}
\label{ch:spanish-ojala}
\hlchaptermodality{129}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can wish for something with ojala, and say where the word came from.}

wa-sha' allah, carried through al-Andalus and kept long after.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ojalá + subjunctive]{ojalá + subjunctive — a wish borrowed through Arabic}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-ojala}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ojalá hables español} means “I hope you speak Spanish” or “May you speak Spanish.” \textbf{Ojalá} expresses the wish by itself. It needs neither a main verb nor \textbf{que} before the subjunctive. Keep the first frame tiny:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ojalá + subjunctive}
\end{quote}

That is a usable modern pattern. It does not make the Arabic source phrase new Spanish vocabulary.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The Real Academia Española records \textbf{ojalá} from Hispanic Arabic \textbf{wa šá lláh}, “and God has willed.” Long contact in al-Andalus carried the expression into Spanish, where its sound and grammatical life changed. You met another Arabic-derived function word in \textbf{hasta}. The historical phrase explains a route; only modern \textbf{ojalá} is available for your Spanish sentences.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Use only modern \textbf{ojalá} as the Spanish trigger.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What follows \textbf{ojalá} in the learned frame? (The \textbf{subjunctive}.) Does it need \textbf{que}? (\textbf{No.}) Which historical language variety carried the word into Spanish? (\textbf{Hispanic Arabic.}) Is the older Arabic phrase usable as new Spanish vocabulary here? (\textbf{No.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — assert the event or want it}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds no vocabulary, plural person, object pronoun, or new clause frame. First decide whether the event is asserted or wanted. Then retrieve only the singular rows you learned.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the bounded map}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{yo / él / ella / usted} & \textbf{tú} \\
\midrule
hablar & hable & hables \\
comer & coma & comas \\
vivir & viva & vivas \\
querer & quiera & quieras \\
poder & pueda & puedas \\
hacer & haga & hagas \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The repeated outer form is not a missing row: first- and third-person singular match. Every plural form waits.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two safe triggers}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Same doer: \textbf{Quiero hablar español.}
  \item Different doer: \textbf{Quiero que hables español.}
  \item Wish by itself: \textbf{Ojalá hables español.}
\end{itemize}

Do not extend these two frames to every emotion, doubt, command, or conjunction yet. More triggers belong in later micro-lessons.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Decide the meaning first; then retrieve only the learned form.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the first meaning choice? (\textbf{Asserted event or wanted event.}) Give the three regular tú forms. (\textbf{Hables, comas, vivas.}) Give the three bounded special tú forms. (\textbf{Quieras, puedas, hagas.}) Name the two safe triggers. (\textbf{Quiero que} for a different doer; \textbf{ojalá} for a wish.) What still waits? (Plural persons, additional irregular verbs, and additional subjunctive triggers.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — you never learned a new stem}

\label{lesson:ES-C18-repaso-el-yo-que-viaja}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}I want you to want.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Quiero que quieras}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four verbs came at you one after another, and each looked like a fresh thing to memorise. Put them in a column and the memorising disappears.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you already said} & \textbf{so you say} \\
\midrule
\emph{vivo} & \emph{viva} \\
\emph{quiero} & \emph{quiera} \\
\emph{puedo} & \emph{pueda} \\
\emph{hago} & \emph{haga} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One move, four times: \textbf{take the \emph{yo} form, drop the \emph{-o}, put \emph{-a} on instead.}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Look at what rode across with the stem.

\emph{Quiero} carries \emph{ie}, and \emph{quiera} keeps it. \emph{Puedo} carries \emph{ue}, and \emph{pueda} keeps it. \emph{Hago} carries a \emph{g} that \emph{hacer} has nowhere else, and \emph{haga} keeps that too.

None of those was a new irregular form. Each was an old one, already paid for, travelling into a new place on the back of the \emph{yo} you had been saying for weeks. That is why the four lessons felt repetitive: they were.

The \emph{-a} is worth one more look. \emph{Vivir} ends in \emph{-ir} and \emph{querer}, \emph{poder} and \emph{hacer} end in \emph{-er}, and all four still land on \emph{-a}, \emph{-as}, \emph{-a}. The two families that stay apart in the present tense stop being two families here.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vivo, viva} · \emph{quiero, quiera} · \emph{puedo, pueda} · \emph{hago, haga}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form do you start from? (\textbf{The \emph{yo} form of the present}.) Where did the \emph{ie} in \emph{quiera} come from? (\emph{\textbf{Quiero}} — it was already there.) How many new stems did these four lessons ask you to learn? (\textbf{None}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
